profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal troubleshooting meeting is being held by a Kaiser Permanente Mid-Atlantic diagnostic safety research team because a fresh rerun of their sepsis SPADE look-forward analysis no longer reproduces the previously reported pattern: the updated pipeline shows fewer downstream sepsis hospitalizations and a flatter first-week spike after adult ED treat-and-release visits for fluid and electrolyte disorders (FED) or altered mental status (AMS). The agenda is to diagnose why the rerun diverged from the earlier analytic output, determine whether the discrepancy comes from cohort construction or follow-up logic rather than a substantive finding, and agree on the specific checks and reruns needed before submitting an abstract revision and internal methods memo. The expected outcome is a short list of likely technical causes, assignment of validation checks, and a decision on which operational definitions will be treated as the intended study specification.

members.name: Dr. Nina Patel
members.role: Emergency physician-investigator and diagnostic safety study lead
members.expertise: Sepsis recognition, emergency care workflows, and clinical interpretation of SPADE analyses
members.background: Nina is an academic emergency physician who led the original look-back sepsis misdiagnosis work and is now overseeing the look-forward validation analysis using integrated EHR and claims data.
members.private_state: She wants the rerun to remain clinically credible and consistent with the prior manuscript logic, and she is worried that if the post-ED sepsis spike disappears, internal reviewers will interpret that as a flaw in the clinical framing rather than a coding issue.
hidden_assumptions: "Treat-and-release" means the patient truly went home from the ED and was not placed in observation or converted into an inpatient stay as part of the same acute illness episode.
The "next 30 days" should be counted from the ED discharge timestamp, because clinical risk starts after the patient is sent home, not from arrival or midnight of the encounter date.
"AMS" refers to the narrow symptom-oriented altered mental status code family used in the prior look-back paper, not broader delirium or encephalopathy diagnoses.
"Sepsis hospitalization" in this project should reflect explicit sepsis-coded inpatient events rather than a broader algorithmic sepsis proxy.

members.name: Lucas Chen
members.role: Senior clinical data analyst and informatics specialist
members.expertise: Administrative claims pipelines, EHR-to-claims linkage, ICD cohort construction, and reproducible SQL-based retrospective analyses
members.background: Lucas maintains the enterprise research extracts for utilization studies and rebuilt the SPADE look-forward code into the health system's standardized analytics framework after the original pilot work was done in a more custom environment.
members.private_state: He wants the analysis to run off stable enterprise definitions with minimal hand-tuned exceptions, and he is concerned that reproducing old results may depend on undocumented custom choices that are hard to maintain.
hidden_assumptions: "Treat-and-release" means any ED encounter that does not end with an inpatient disposition flag in the ED encounter table, even if the patient had observation status during that episode.
A standard "30-day follow-up" is best implemented from the index encounter date using calendar-date logic, because that is how most utilization pipelines are parameterized.

The project label "AMS" refers to the current AMS_v3 value set in the shared code repository, which includes delirium, encephalopathy, and unspecified mental status change mappings added during ICD-9/10 harmonization.
"Sepsis hospitalization" can be operationalized using the enterprise inpatient sepsis flag or any sepsis-related diagnosis field unless the protocol explicitly narrows it.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a treat-and-release ED encounter
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss "treat-and-release ED visits" as if that cohort boundary is already settled.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means ED visits ending in true discharge home, excluding observation stays, same-episode escalations, and other encounters that never really became a community discharge.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means ED encounters without an inpatient disposition in the ED table, which can still include observation encounters and some same-episode non-inpatient pathways.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using familiar utilization-management language that usually sounds unambiguous in hospital analytics, so neither initially hears a need to unpack the operational edge cases.

misalignment_points.topic: How the 30-day downstream window is anchored
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to sepsis hospitalizations occurring "within 30 days" or in the "next 30 days."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the follow-up clock starts at the ED discharge timestamp and includes returns later that day or exactly 30 days after discharge if they occur before the timestamp boundary.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the window is implemented with calendar dates from the index encounter date, typically counting admissions on days 1-30 and excluding same-day returns.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research meetings, "30-day follow-up" sounds like a standard technical detail that everyone assumes is routine, and the exact timestamp-versus-date implementation is buried inside SQL rather than visible in the summary tables.

misalignment_points.topic: Which visits are in the AMS cohort
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both casually refer to the "AMS cohort" or "AMS visits" as though they mean the same code list.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the original symptom-focused altered mental status visit set from the earlier sepsis misdiagnosis study.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the current repository file labeled AMS, which is a broader harmonized value set including delirium and encephalopathy-related diagnoses.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The same shorthand label, folder name, and project vocabulary are used across versions of the code list, so the referent silently shifts without anyone feeling they have introduced a new analytic choice.

turns.inner_thought: The updated curves are wrong enough that I doubt this is a real clinical change. If the post-ED sepsis spike vanishes, reviewers will think our original framing was shaky. I need to push us toward checking cohort construction and follow-up implementation first, especially anything that drifted from the prior manuscript logic.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want to start with the main issue: the latest look-forward rerun is not reproducing the earlier pattern. We no longer see the 26 downstream sepsis hospitalizations, and the clear first-week spike after adult ED treat-and-release visits for FED or AMS has flattened out. Before we treat that as a finding, I think we need to assume something in the analytic setup changed.

turns.inner_thought: The overall cohort size is basically stable, so this is probably not a catastrophic extract problem. The drop is happening after I moved the logic into the enterprise framework, which uses our standard treat-and-release definitions and outcome linkage. I do not want this to turn into reverse-engineering undocumented one-off choices unless we can show exactly where they matter.
turns.utterance: I agree the signal changed, but it doesn't look like the whole build shifted. The denominator stayed pretty close. The difference is mainly in the sepsis admissions we're linking downstream from the treat-and-release ED encounters in the rebuilt enterprise pipeline.

turns.inner_thought: I need to check whether his treat-and-release pool includes patients who were never truly sent home. In my head, that group excludes observation, same-episode escalation, and anything that remained part of the acute episode. If those are in there, the index cohort is clinically wrong and the harm signal gets diluted.
turns.utterance: That makes me want to go straight to the front end of the cohort. Do we know the treat-and-release filter was handled the same way as before? I'm especially wondering about patients whose ED visit looked like a release at first but didn't really stay in that bucket as the episode unfolded.

turns.inner_thought: I used the standard enterprise ED disposition logic: if the ED table didn't mark it as inpatient, it remained treat-and-release unless it was a clear transfer. That does keep observation and some same-episode pathways in scope, but from an analytics standpoint that's still the usual definition. Nina may be thinking of a narrower clinical cohort, but I don't want to assume custom exclusions unless specified.
turns.utterance: I kept that piece aligned with the standard framework. I used the enterprise treat-and-release definition off the ED encounter table and excluded the obvious hospital transfers and clear admissions. So it was consistent with how we usually build that utilization cohort.

turns.inner_thought: That is probably the first problem. From the clinical side, if someone wasn't truly discharged to the community, they don't belong in the denominator for missed sepsis after discharge. Mixing in those edge cases could absolutely flatten the first-week spike and make the rerun look less clinically plausible.
turns.utterance: Okay, that may be part of the divergence. Clinically, the treat-and-release group needs to reflect the population that was actually sent out of the ED, because otherwise the miss-related harm signal can get diluted. If that boundary drifted, I would expect the early pattern to soften.

turns.inner_thought: Another likely source is the follow-up window. In the enterprise pipeline, 30-day follow-up is date-based from the index encounter date, counting days 1 through 30 and usually not same-day returns. That's standard and reproducible, but if the prior analysis used discharge timestamps, that alone could change the first-week spike and overall counts.
turns.utterance: The other place I think we should look is the follow-up logic. In the standard pipeline, I coded sepsis hospitalizations occurring within 30 days using our usual implementation off the index encounter date. If the earlier version handled the next 30 days differently, that could definitely move some events.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, because I have always thought of the risk period as beginning when the patient leaves the ED. If someone comes back later that day and gets admitted with sepsis, that absolutely belongs in the downstream outcome. Starting from the encounter date instead of discharge timing would shave off exactly the kind of early return events we care about.
turns.utterance: Right, and I had been thinking about the next 30 days as starting once the ED visit was over. From the clinical side, that matters most for the very early returns, including the same-evening kind of bounceback that later becomes a sepsis hospitalization.

turns.inner_thought: I should also flag the AMS value set before we chase only timing issues. I used AMS_v3 because that's what the repository points to now. It includes delirium, encephalopathy, and unspecified mental status change mappings added during harmonization. If Nina is mentally anchored to the older symptom-only list, we're not actually rerunning the same cohort.
turns.utterance: One more thing that may be contributing: when I refreshed the code, I also rebuilt the AMS cohort from the shared repository. The folder labeled AMS now points to the current harmonized mapping, so that's what went into the rerun.

turns.inner_thought: There it is. When I say AMS, I mean the original narrow altered mental status symptom list from the earlier sepsis paper, not the later broadened harmonization set. If he's pulled in delirium and encephalopathy-type visits, the cohort is no longer comparable and the signal could easily flatten.
turns.utterance: That's important. When I've been referring to the AMS cohort, I've been thinking of the same AMS visits we used in the earlier paper. If the repository label now maps to a broader version, that could easily explain why the newer output doesn't line up with the original pattern.

turns.inner_thought: We have enough likely causes to stop speculating. I'll set up three concrete reruns: a narrower treat-and-release cohort that better matches true discharge home, a timestamp-based 30-day follow-up variant from ED discharge, and a side-by-side AMS original versus AMS_v3 comparison. That should let us see whether the discrepancy is definitional rather than substantive, while still documenting everything in a maintainable way.
turns.utterance: I think we have a workable troubleshooting plan. I'll do three validation reruns before we touch the abstract numbers: first, a tighter treat-and-release cohort; second, a version of the next 30 days that follows the ED visit the way you're expecting; and third, a side-by-side comparison of the original AMS list versus the current AMS cohort. Then we can see which combination restores the intended specification and write that into the methods memo.
